# Field Guide: Preparing a Home for a 72-Hour Power Outage

This guide prepares an ordinary household to manage safely and comfortably through a power outage of up to seventy-two hours, in a temperate climate with no backup generator. Work through the sections in order; the earlier ones matter most.

## Water

Store four litres of water per person per day — twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours. Half is for drinking, half for cooking and basic hygiene. Use food-grade containers, keep them out of direct sunlight, and replace stored water every six months. If a storm is forecast and you have warning, also fill the bathtub; bathtub water is for flushing toilets and washing, never drinking.

## Food

Keep a dedicated shelf of non-perishable food for three days: canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, and shelf-stable milk. Choose foods needing no cooking, and own a manual can opener, since an electric one is useless. Eat perishable refrigerator food first, then freezer food, and only then the emergency shelf.

## Refrigerator and freezer

An unopened refrigerator keeps food safe about four hours. A full freezer holds a safe temperature about forty-eight hours, but a half-full one only about twenty-four, so keep the freezer consolidated and full, even if some space holds containers of frozen water. Keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a reminder note to each. Discard any perishable food left more than two hours above four degrees Celsius; when in doubt, throw it out.

## Light

Use battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps as your primary light, and avoid candles entirely, a leading cause of house fires during outages. Store at least one light per person plus two spare sets of batteries for each. Keep one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen, placed where they can be found in the dark.

## Heat and safety

Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window; each produces carbon monoxide, which is odourless and can be fatal. Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep. In cold weather, pick one small room on a south-facing side, close its door, and gather everyone there; layered clothing and blankets beat any improvised heater. If the indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot stay warm, relocate to a warming centre or a neighbour's home.

## Communication and information

Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts, and learn your local emergency station's frequency before the outage. Charge every phone and power bank whenever a storm is forecast; a full modern twenty-thousand-milliamp-hour power bank recharges a typical phone roughly four times. Put your phone in low-power mode as the outage starts, and agree in advance on one out-of-area contact everyone will text, since texts cross congested networks more reliably than voice calls.

## Medical needs

Keep a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication, rotating them to stay in date. Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally stays usable at room temperature up to twenty-eight days, but confirm the rule for your medication with a pharmacist beforehand. Write your pharmacy, doctor, and poison-control numbers on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book.

## When the power returns

Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, so the grid can stabilise. Check the freezer: food still holding ice crystals can be safely refrozen. Restock everything used within one week, starting with water and batteries. Finally, write a one-page note on what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one gap before the next outage.
hardConstraintNote: Remains a self-contained instruction document (GR-3): identical title, all nine markdown section headers in original order, purely imperative field instructions, and every actionable number/item/step intact — a reader with only this text can execute the full 72-hour preparation without the original.

rationale: Single per-sentence pass over a scratch copy, no reorganization (matches the low-cost line-editor lever in frontier.leverCosts). Removed only connective filler and framing throat-clearing ('This guide explains how to...', 'Good choices are...', 'because each of these produces...'), converted passive to active ('should be discarded' -> 'Discard'), and hyphenated compound modifiers ('twenty thousand milliamp-hours' -> 'twenty-thousand-milliamp-hour'). NO fact deleted: all nine sections retained in original order; every quantity (4 L/person/day, 12 L, 72 h, six months, 3 days, 4 h, 48 h, 24 h, 2 h, 4 C, one light/person, two spare battery sets, 10 C, 20,000 mAh, ~4 recharges, 7-day supply, 28 days, 5 minutes, one week, one-page), every listed item (six food items; camping stove/barbecue/generator; pharmacy/doctor/poison-control), and every ordered step (fridge->freezer->shelf; wait 5 min->check freezer->restock->write note) survive verbatim in meaning. Lands at the frontier's stated line-editor ceiling (~615) — the removable connective filler and intro framing, with all numeric facts kept for the held-out 8/8 gate.
